column24:
Dear young owner,

My niece showed me the reviews of your little restaurant on her phone. A countryside shop serving food from six countries? I had to write.

I'm Malai. I've run a kitchen in Bangkok for thirty years, but I started at my mother's dessert cart. Mango sticky rice was what children begged for, and what tired mothers bought to say "you did well today."

Steam the sticky rice until it shines, pour warm coconut cream over it, and let it rest. Slice the mango just before serving.

Sweet things are a small kindness. Give them often.

Dear owner,

Malai again. I hear your mango sticky rice makes people smile. Good. Now something with a little fire.

Tom yum was my father's cure for everything. A cold, a bad day, a broken heart. He would stand over the pot and say, "If your nose doesn't run, it isn't tom yum."

Lemongrass bruised so it gives everything, lime added at the very end, and shrimp that only just turn pink. Never let them boil too long.

Sour, spicy, salty, a little sweet. Life is never only one taste.

column24:
Dear owner,

It's Malai again. I hear the basil pork is doing well. Good!

Pad Thai is the dish every visitor asks me for, so you should have it too. When I was young I thought it was too simple to be proud of. Then a tourist cried at my table because it reminded her of her honeymoon. Simple food carries big memories.

Soak the noodles, don't boil them. Shrimp, tofu, egg, then the sauce: tamarind, fish sauce, palm sugar. Bean sprouts at the very end so they stay crisp.

Don't let anyone tell you a small shop can't be a great one.

column24:
To the owner,

Forgive the sudden letter. I read about your shop online, a place where one cook serves six countries. In Japan we say a person should master one thing. You seem to be trying six. I respect that.

I am Kenji Morita. I fry tonkatsu in a small shop near a train station in Osaka. Students, salarymen, old men alone. They all sit at the same counter.

Pound the pork, bread it carefully, fry it twice if you must. Shred the cabbage so fine it looks like snow.

Simple food, done properly, is never simple.

Hello,

A traveler who ate at your shop left a long review online. He said the food tasted like someone cared. That is rare. I wanted to write to the person who cooks like that.

I am Lin Wei. Before I owned a restaurant, I washed dishes in one for six years. The chef paid us in egg fried rice made from yesterday's rice. It was the best meal of my day.

Cold rice, a very hot wok, egg first, then rice, and keep everything moving.

Nothing in a kitchen should be wasted. Not rice, not people.

Hello, my friend,

May I call you that now? Lin Wei here.

Kung pao chicken is loud food. Chili, peanuts, a hot wok shouting at you. My wife says it is the only time I raise my voice.

Cut the chicken small, toast the chilies until they darken but never burn, and add the peanuts last so they stay crisp.

When your shop gets busy and noisy, do not be afraid of it. A loud kitchen is a living kitchen.

Ciao!

I am Giulia, from a small trattoria in Rome. A customer told me about your shop. "Six countries in one kitchen," he said, shaking his head. Then he said the food was good. So, I write.

Aglio e olio is what Roman cooks eat at midnight, after service, when everyone is too tired to talk. Pasta, garlic, chili, good oil. Nothing else.

Cook the garlic slowly until it is golden, never brown. Save a little pasta water. It makes everything come together.

The dishes with the fewest things have nowhere to hide.

Ciao again!

Your carbonara is getting good reviews. Brava! Now we go further.

Margherita was named after a queen, but I learned it from a very loud baker in Naples who shouted at me every day for a whole summer. On my last day he gave me his dough knife and said I was "not hopeless." The highest praise of my life.

Flour, water, yeast, and time. Stretch by hand, never a rolling pin. Tomato, mozzarella, fresh basil, a very hot oven.

Sometimes the people who push you hardest believe in you the most.

Ciao again!

Giulia here. Your garlic pasta has fans, I hear. Brava! Now a true Roman classic.

Carbonara has started more arguments in my family than politics. Cream or no cream? (No cream.) My nonna would leave the table if you asked.

Take the pan off the heat before the egg goes in. Toss fast, add pasta water, and let the hard cheese melt into a silky sauce. Too hot and you have scrambled eggs.

Some rules are worth keeping. Most of them came from someone's nonna.

column24:
Hey there!

Name's Dan. I run a diner off Route 9, been flipping burgers for twenty-two years. My daughter found your place online and said, "Dad, this kid's doing what you did." So here I am, writing a letter like it's 1985.

Before the diner I drove trucks. Lonely work. The best part of any day was a cheeseburger at some roadside joint where nobody asked me questions.

Smash the beef thin on a hot griddle, cheese on right after the flip, toast the bun. Lettuce, tomato, pickles. Don't overthink it.

Hey again!

Dan here. Heard your place is getting real busy. Proud of you, kid, and I don't even know you.

This pie is my late wife's. Mary baked it every Sunday for the diner, and folks drove an hour just for a slice. After she passed, I couldn't make it for two years. Then one day a regular asked for "Mary's pie," and I figured she'd want it served, not missed.

Cold butter in the crust, apples with sugar and cinnamon, bake till the juice bubbles.

Some recipes are meant to keep going.

Hola, amigo,

My grandson reads restaurant reviews from all over the world, and yours made him laugh: "Tacos in the countryside, made by someone who isn't even Mexican." Then he said they were good. So now I must help you make them better.

I am Rosa Delgado, a cocinera from Oaxaca. When I was young, I sold fish tacos on the beach to fishermen coming home at dawn.

Fry or grill the fish quickly, warm the tortillas until they puff, and finish with a squeeze of lime.

Food is for sharing. Never forget it.

column24:
Hola again,

Rosa here. My grandson says your shop is busier now. Bueno! Then you are ready for tamales.

Tamales are never made alone. At Christmas my whole family sits around the table, spreading corn dough on husks, filling, folding, laughing, arguing. Three hundred tamales in one afternoon.

Spread the dough thin, fill with pork and chili, fold tight, and steam them standing up.

If you ever make tamales alone, invite someone next time. They taste better that way.

Hola again,

Rosa here. My grandson says your little shop has many reviews now. Qué bien!

Enchiladas are what I cook for big family Sundays. Twenty people, three generations, everyone arguing and laughing. When I was young, I wanted quiet. Now that my house is quiet, I miss the noise.

Roll chicken in warm tortillas, cover with red chili sauce and cheese, and bake until it bubbles.

You don't have to love crowds. But leave a little room at your table, just in case.

Hello again,

Lin Wei writing. I read that your shop has more regulars now. Regulars are the true reputation of a kitchen.

Roast duck was the dish my old chef never let me touch. For three years I only watched. When he finally let me roast one, he said nothing, ate a piece, and walked away. The next morning my name was on the duck schedule.

Brush the skin with honey, let it dry, and roast until it crackles. Patience is the main ingredient.

Some approval is quiet. Learn to hear it.

Cara amica,

Giulia once more. My cousin from Genoa heard I was writing to you and insisted I send this one. She says I make pesto "like a Roman," which is not a compliment.

Basil, a little cheese, good oil, crushed together until it turns bright green. Never cook the pesto. Toss it with the hot pasta and let the warmth do the work.

My cousin and I still argue about it every summer. We also eat it together every summer.

Family is the people you argue with and still share a table with.

Hey again!

Dan here. My waitress, Darlene, read about your place and asked me to send you her grandma's recipe. Darlene has worked at my diner for twenty-two years, so when she asks, I listen.

Peach cobbler isn't fancy. Ripe peaches, a buttery batter poured over the top, baked until the edges go golden and the fruit bubbles through.

Serve it warm. Ice cream if you've got it.

The best recipes in my diner came from the people who work there. Remember to ask yours.

column24:
My dear,

Rosa here. You have come a long way, so I send you something from my heart: mole.

In Oaxaca, a family's mole is its signature. My grandmother's had more than twenty ingredients, and she never wrote them down. I learned by standing next to her for years, tasting, failing, tasting again.

Chili, chocolate, spices, toasted slowly, ground, and simmered for hours until dark and deep. Serve it over chicken.

Some things can only be taught by standing beside someone. I hope these letters were a little like that.

column24:
Dear friend,

Giulia here, from the coast this time. I am on holiday near Naples, and I ate a salad so simple it made me cry a little.

Caprese is only three things: buffalo mozzarella, ripe tomato, fresh basil. The colours of our flag. If even one of them is poor, the whole dish fails.

Use mozzarella from buffalo milk, as fresh as you can find. Slice, layer, a little salt and oil. Do not cook anything.

When the ingredients are honest, the cook only has to step aside.
